When should local checks be reconciled in conversation, an operating view or a separate retained account? **Adopt** a shared question with recoverable contributing claims, using R10's operational/coordination practice and [OPS.4][OPS4]. **Adapt** the communication arrangement to who will rely on those claims and when. Direct exchange and an already adequate operating view are serious alternatives to another maintained record.

Sections 4.1–4.3 choose the arrangement for the same needed session conclusion. In §5, participants who can inspect the same materials and act together can resolve the question in conversation. A later technician cannot depend on having heard that exchange; the existing operating view can preserve W, the changed room, still-valid material grounds and missing room observations. Adding a second report provides no further needed distinction when that view is sufficient. Accept the extra recording and update effort only when a later consequential use still lacks its subjects, grounds or changes.

R7's dependency cases and R10's views supply the practice comparison, while Gawande's open team exchanges supply a coordination candidate for trouble outside fixed questions. These accounts explain why a shared conversation can be the useful action; they do not measure the cost of every arrangement. [Anthropic's account][ANTHROPIC1] supplies bounded engineering evidence for retaining criteria and progress across agent sessions. It motivates recoverable continuation, not a universal reporting format or cadence.

The defect overcome is a lost local-to-whole dependency or an unrecoverable handover, not a low completion percentage. **Reject** aggregation of labels as the substitute for that relation. The selected arrangement deliberately trades communication and maintenance effort for the specific later reliance it enables; where an existing exchange or view suffices, it adds no new record. Reopen the choice when a new participant, delay, changed work or tool prevents recovery of a consequential connection, or when duplicate maintenance outweighs its remaining use.

### CHK.5:12 - Relations

CHK.4 supplies local answers and their grounds. CHK.1 supplies questions about the shared result, CHK.6 tests uncertain criteria, and CHK.3 arranges participants' access and interaction.

[OPS.3][OPS3] distinguishes operating subjects, [OPS.4][OPS4] supplies a recoverable shared operating account, and [ADM.13][ADM13] supplies administrative record fitness. [FPF B.1.5][B15] supplies Method composition and [A.15.10][A1510] changed-premise recovery. Their general accounts remain external; this Method specializes their contributions to checklist answers used across shared work.

### CHK.5:End

## CHK.6 - Qualify Checklist Criteria and Checking Means


### CHK.6:1 - Problem frame

**Use this when** a proposed criterion or checking means may fail to distinguish the difference that matters. This is common with inherited lists, generated criteria, model judgements, new tools and changed operating conditions. A checker can say “pass” while an importer replaces A17 with 1.

This Method establishes a bounded basis for using a criterion and its checking means, or returns a counterexample or unresolved qualification question. Start with one claim the proposed check is supposed to support and one plausible case where it could be wrong.

Reuse an applicable qualification when available. A second agent, a formal experiment or a broad benchmark is useful only when it answers a live uncertainty at worthwhile cost.

### CHK.6:2 - Problem

A criterion can be irrelevant, vague or based on a mistaken description. A checker can implement a sensible criterion badly or observe a convenient proxy. Agreement among judges and high aggregate scores can hide the individual failure that matters to the work.

The problem is to examine both the criterion and the means of checking it before placing more reliance on their answers than the evidence supports. This differs from selecting which questions belong in the aid and from checking the actual subject on one occasion.

### CHK.6:3 - Forces

| Tension | Practical implication |
| --- | --- |
| Useful coverage and cheap proxies | Test the consequential distinction rather than the easiest correlated signal. |
| Improvement speed and qualification cost | Start with a discriminating counterexample; expand only for the intended reliance. |
| Human judgement and executable checks | Use the means capable of observing the relevant property; neither is universally superior. |
| Aggregate evaluation and individual failures | Inspect the cases that could defeat the intended use. |
| Stable reuse and changing models or tools | Bound the qualification and identify what would reopen it. |

### CHK.6:4 - Solution

#### CHK.6:4.1 - Recover the claim, basis and intended reliance

Name the criterion, the question it interprets and the subject of that question. Recover the description and the assumption connecting it to useful work. Use [ME.3][ME3] when the criterion needs construction from the subject and situation.

Then name the checking means: a person applying a judgement, a comparison script, an observation tool or a model-based evaluator. What does it actually observe or consume? What answer does it produce? What will another person or system infer from that answer? [ADM.7][ADM7] supplies claim-checking distinctions from administrative practice. A method name or test file is not itself proof that the intended check occurred.

For a model judge, include the supplied evidence and instructions, the criteria grouped in each call, and any rule combining repeated verdicts when these can change the relied-on answer.

Separate two uncertainties. A criterion can faithfully express the description while the description poorly serves the work. A checking means can also fail to apply that otherwise useful criterion. Investigate the uncertainty that changes the intended use.

A cheap indirect signal can justify further examination without certifying the larger result when it passes. An obsolete edition label on the card box can prompt inspection of its contents; a current label alone does not establish that every card was replaced. Name this intended inference and next move. Challenge both false reassurance and unnecessary alarms. If people can satisfy the visible signal while bypassing the substantive work, examine whether the signal remains informative for the intended use.

#### CHK.6:4.2 - Construct a discriminating challenge

Choose cases with known or competently established differences relevant to the criterion. Include a satisfactory case and a plausible failure. Vary the property of interest while holding irrelevant differences small enough to interpret the result. For a subjective criterion, recover the judgement basis and a meaningful disagreement rather than inventing a false objective threshold.

Predict which answers those differences support before inspecting the checker output. Then compare the outputs with adequate grounds for those expected distinctions. A false pass and a false failure can have different costs; inspect both where they affect the work.

Where a rubric may drive the verdict independently of the subject, also hold the subject facts fixed and change the question. Establish what answer the new predicate supports before asking the checker. A reversed condition can call for the opposite answer; if only wording changes and the question stays the same, the expected answer stays the same. This distinction tests responsiveness to meaning without requiring every wording change to reverse a result.

When uncertainty concerns the judging arrangement, compare it on those grounded cases with a cheaper or less interfering alternative. Grouping criteria can save calls; separating them can reveal interference. Repetition and a rule for combining verdicts may reduce sampling instability, but repeated agreement cannot correct a consistent error or supply independent truth. Select the arrangement from consequential errors and total effort; repeat only when that comparison can change reliance.

If the receiving use consumes a total or percentage, examine what that number means and how the questions affect it. Splitting one easy condition into ten items can increase its influence without improving the subject. Ten successful formatting checks may conceal one failed catalogue-preservation check. Challenge the implied priorities, duplicate contributions and treatment of missing answers. Keep consequential answers visible. Where a numerical aggregate is actually needed, [FPF A.19.ULSAM][ULSAM] governs the admitted measures and lawful aggregation; a convenient average does not supply its own justification.

Start cheaply. One counterexample can defeat an overbroad claim. Use a direct executable comparison when the question and observable property admit it. A selective rubric or pairwise judgement can help with an interpretive or relative question, but choosing the better of two results does not establish that either meets an absolute condition. Qualify that judging arrangement on cases whose consequential answers have adequate independent grounds. Compare false passes, false failures and obtaining those grounds as well as the cost per judgement. Broader reliance may call for representative cases, independent judgement, executable observation or a field trial through [ME.11][ME11]. Choose another reader or agent when it supplies a materially different basis, expertise or observation. Mere duplication of the same unsupported inference does not establish independence.

When work is repeatedly optimized against a score, compare earlier and later actual results on consequential characteristics and suitable new cases. A rising score can reward surface changes while the intended result deteriorates. For the importer, a more persuasive success report leaves identifier loss unchanged. Inspect the proposed shortcut and obtain evidence beyond the optimized signal. A stronger second model can help investigate disagreement, but its score still needs grounds and does not become ground truth by rank.

#### CHK.6:4.3 - State the bounded result and a return condition

State what the qualification supports: which criterion, checking means, cases, conditions and receiving use it covers. State detected defects and residual uncertainty in terms that change action. A narrow successful probe does not establish all-domain accuracy.

If the criterion misses a work question, return to CHK.1. If the form corrupts its meaning, return to CHK.2. If access or capability is missing, return to CHK.3 or its supplier. If the checker fails, repair, replace or restrict its use and repeat the affected challenge. Compare the gain with the qualification and operating cost through [ME.14][ME14].

Keep the qualification separate from actual subject answers. CHK.4 still establishes what is true of the subject on its occasion. Reopen qualification when a material criterion, model, tool, observation route or operating condition changes, or when a new counterexample defeats its scope. Changed evidence, instructions, criterion grouping or verdict combination can trigger this even with the same model and criterion. Retain qualification for the unaffected observations and inferences. Stop when further investigation cannot improve the intended reliance at worthwhile cost, and preserve the limit rather than extending the claim.

### CHK.6:5 - Archetypal Grounding

A team describes an importer as preserving item identifiers, reporting duplicate identifiers and retaining the previous catalogue when parsing fails. The description embodies assumptions about the team's use. A proposed generated check asks only whether an input file was accepted.

That check establishes none of the three described properties. A17 can become 1 during an otherwise successful import. A successful run also says nothing about duplicate reporting or the state after a parse failure.

The team constructs these qualification cases:

| Case | Distinction to establish | Observation capable of supporting it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Valid catalogue with identifier A17 | Identifier preserved, rather than replaced or normalized unexpectedly. | Compare the input identifier with the stored identifier for the corresponding item. |
| Two records with the same identifier | The described duplicate report occurs for that input. | Inspect the returned report and its association with the duplicate records. |
| Malformed input with a known prior catalogue | Parse failure leaves the prior catalogue intact. | Observe the failure and compare the relevant catalogue state before and after it. |

These are three separate questions. A candidate checker that observes only an exit code cannot settle the third unless an independently established relation makes that code sufficient for the stated use. The team tests its proposed before/after comparison against a deliberately altered catalogue and an unchanged one. If it passes both, it has failed the intended discrimination; if it distinguishes them, that supports the comparison for those cases.

Complement that changed-catalogue challenge with a changed-question challenge. Use a constructed fixture whose before and after catalogues are both C. For these fixed facts, “Are the before and after catalogue contents identical?” has the expected answer **Yes**, while “Do the after contents differ from the before contents?” has the expected answer **No**. “Do both snapshots contain the same catalogue content?” preserves the first question and therefore its expected Yes. These answers follow from the fixture before any checker is run. A checker that returns the same verdict for the opposite conditions misses the question; one that changes the first answer merely because it is reworded is unstable on that case. Passing these contrasts supports only this bounded discrimination.

To examine grouped judging, give a model the same before and after snapshots C, plus a report headed “Import summary”. Before any output, content identity has expected **Yes**, and the presence of that heading has its separate expected **Yes**. Compare the identity verdict when asked alone and when asked alongside the heading question, with the same evidence supplied. The extra question changes neither snapshot nor the identity predicate. Repeat the contrast with a fixture whose after snapshot changes A17 to 1: identity is then **No** in both arrangements, while the heading answer stays Yes. If grouping changes either identity verdict, investigate or restrict that arrangement; do not average the two distinct questions into a pass. Combining repeated identity verdicts still has to answer to these fixture facts. Where grouped judging preserves the needed distinctions at lower cost, keep it. For actual stored data, an adequate direct comparison remains the cheaper starting choice.

A known malformed-input case with an unobserved post-state remains unresolved. Tool failure is not an importer failure or success. Local parser correctness does not settle the encompassing response and catalogue state; CHK.5 connects those contributions.

For the workshop display, “readable” may be judged from a desktop preview while participants will read the projected content from the back of a room. Qualification varies the viewing condition relevant to the exercise and asks a representative participant to interpret the actual content. A font-size threshold can be a useful local proxy only if its basis supports that use. Reconsider that proxy if glare or contrast makes text unreadable despite the chosen size.

Both examples are constructed probes. They illustrate how to challenge a claim, not measured checker performance.

### CHK.6:6 - Bias-Annotation

People tend to invent tests that confirm their implementation. Generated criteria and generated answers can share the same blind spot. Recover a failure from the receiving work, seek an unlike case where it matters, and distinguish the data used to tune a checker from the evidence used to judge its broader use.

A benchmark's accessible cases can underrepresent the domain or participants who bear false failures. Make that limit part of the reliance decision.

### CHK.6:7 - Conformance Checklist

Inspect the qualification's actual claim and probes:

- Are criterion, checking means, subject and receiving inference separately recoverable?
- Do the challenge cases vary a consequential property with adequate grounds for the expected distinction?
- Have false passes, false failures and unresolved observation been interpreted at their actual costs?
- Does any independent contribution supply a different basis rather than repeated agreement?
- Is the resulting reliance bounded, with material change and counterexample triggers for reconsideration?

### CHK.6:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them

| Failure | Repair |
| --- | --- |
| A fluent generated rubric is treated as qualified. | Recover provenance and challenge a consequential distinction. |
| Two agreeing agents establish an unobserved fact. | Obtain an adequate observation or a judgement supported by different grounds. |
| A high average hides a decisive false pass. | Inspect the case and receiving inference that the intended use cannot tolerate. |
| Training reward is treated as runtime assurance. | Test the actual current checking arrangement and subject question. |
| A checker is qualified once for all future models and tools. | Reopen the affected scope when observation or judgement behavior changes. |

### CHK.6:9 - Consequences

The Method can replace an attractive but uninformative check with a defensible, limited one. A single counterexample may prevent large misplaced reliance. Qualification also costs representative data, judgement and maintenance. Some questions remain uncertain or too expensive to settle; the useful outcome can be a smaller reliance claim or a different work arrangement.

### CHK.6:10 - Architectural Rationale

Qualification is independently triggered when the adequacy of criteria or checking means becomes uncertain. Folding it into every ordinary use wastes effort; omitting it from design lets repeated unsupported answers accumulate.

An applicable prior qualification can settle the uncertainty. Otherwise begin with a concrete difference and scale the evidence to the intended reliance, using direct executable tests or competent human judgement as appropriate.

### CHK.6:11 - SoTA-Echoing

Which checking means and qualification effort fit the intended reliance? **Adopt** a direct comparison for an explicit observable property; **adapt** selective rubric or pairwise judging for a genuinely interpretive or relative question, with discriminating cases when its adequacy is uncertain. These are serious alternatives, not successive compulsory stages. In §§4.2 and 5, inspecting identifier or catalogue equality supplies the relevant grounds directly. Asking a model for a persuasive overall score adds cost without settling those properties. Pairwise judging can instead help choose between two explanations, but the preferred one still needs a separate answer to an absolute suitability question.

[Selective Checklist Evaluation][SELECTIVE] supplies a current rival to full-rubric/direct scoring, with effects that differ by setting and comparison mode. It warrants choosing and qualifying the mode for the receiving question, not declaring one universally superior. The study by [Hong and colleagues](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.12835v1) supplies counterevidence about detail and uneven emphasis in generated criteria. Section 4.2 therefore examines consequential errors, missing answers and induced weighting alongside judgement cost. The extra qualification is worthwhile when it can defeat misplaced reliance or select better means; an applicable prior qualification remains sufficient for its unchanged scope.

The study by [Bagaria and colleagues](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.02942v1) supplies bounded counterevidence about judges responding to changed answers and reversed criteria. Its generated and qualitatively inspected contrasts leave uncertainty about some expected verdicts. The adaptation in §§4.2 and 5 fixes expected answers from a simple fixture, then varies subject facts or question meaning separately. [RIPD](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.13576v1) supplies a further benchmark-versus-target counterexample motivating examination after rubric edits; it does not qualify a particular deployed judge.

For single, grouped or repeated model judgements, **adapt** protocol comparison to the consequential uncertainty in §§4.1–4.3 and the fixed-fixture case in §5. [RuVerBench v2](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.29920v2) supplies counterevidence about prompting, grouping and voting under long research/coding contexts; its selected binary cases exclude substantial ambiguity. [PReMISE v1](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.30803v1) separates stability from preference fit and robustness under model-mediated evaluation. Neither determines this deployment's best arrangement. Compare saved calls with consequential errors and examination effort; retain adequate prior qualification, and reopen its affected scope when a changed arrangement can alter a relied-on answer.

[AutoChecklist][AUTOCHECKLIST] and [RLCF][RLCF] supply criterion refinement and checklist-feedback training alternatives. **Reject** their benchmark or training gains as substitutes for qualifying this checker. [CHERRL](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.04923v1) and [Rubric Dropout](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.11669v1) expose proxy exploitation and divergence in bounded training settings; the latter's single-run configurations and fallible external judge limit the result. Its training intervention gives no general reason to omit operational checks. Section 4.2 instead examines actual results and new cases beyond the optimized signal.

The deliberate trade-off is the cost of obtaining discriminating grounds against the cost of a consequential false answer. None of these studies supplies a common error/cost ranking for every domain. [Anthropic's harness-design account][ANTHROPIC2] supplies a worked calibration candidate as models and tools change; [ME.11][ME11] and [ME.14][ME14] guide the local trial and worth comparison when the choice remains consequential. Reopen qualification for a material criterion, tool or use change, an unexplained verdict on a known contrast, or a cheaper adequate observation.

### CHK.6:12 - Relations

CHK.1 supplies proposed work questions and receives coverage corrections. CHK.2 preserves qualified meanings, CHK.3 makes observations accessible, CHK.4 performs actual checks, and CHK.5 interprets their combined use. [FPF A.19.ULSAM][ULSAM] is a conditional return when the receiving use needs numerical aggregation; ordinary separate answers require no such calculation.

[ME.3][ME3] supplies criterion construction, [ME.11][ME11] representative trial, [ME.14][ME14] worth appraisal, and [ADM.7][ADM7] checking. Qualification uses these results for the specific uncertainty in checklist criteria or means; it does not replace those Methods.

### CHK.6:End

# Applications

## From a recurring omission to a useful aid

An organizer repeatedly receives physically complete seminar cards containing wording from an earlier exercise. The facilitator can explain the exercise, and the packer can count and inspect cards; neither currently sees the whole question at the useful moment.

Begin with [CHK.1](#chk1---select-checklist-questions-for-a-work-result) if useful questions are missing. The first result is a question set tied to the work, or a clear statement of the domain judgement still needed. With adequate questions already available, start at the contribution that is missing. The mantra below follows the aid through use and appraisal; a sufficient direct question can end the search immediately.

> **Mantra — from omission to a worthwhile aid:** Name the omission and the work result it threatens. Reuse adequate questions, forms and checking means; obtain only what is missing. Tie each question to its subject, description and intended use. Make an answer possible at the useful moment, challenge uncertain criteria or means, and answer from adequate grounds. Keep the answer, the decision and the work distinct. Connect answers that affect the whole. After change or interruption, recover the question and its grounds; reconsider only affected reliance. Compare the aid's contribution with its full burden. Improve what obstructs useful work, or retire the aid when a simpler arrangement suffices.

The worked case below explains those conditional moves. Resume at the unresolved contribution after interruption; if the questions have been answered but the aid's worth remains unknown, continue with **Worth and improvement** and [ME.14][ME14].

**Selection.** CHK.1 separates the physical-set description from the assumption that this set will serve the exercise. The three selected questions concern contents/readability, wording and assembly. A separate exercise trial addresses instructional usefulness. The result is a bounded question set with actual sources for its answers.

**Construction.** CHK.2 puts the set and description reference once above the questions. The packing view carries count/readability and assembly; the facilitator's view carries wording comparison. Both retain S and v2. The answer forms allow a supported negative or an unresolved question. The transposed example in CHK.2 shows the same answers without changing their subject.

**Fitting.** CHK.3 puts the questions in the preparation workspace, with the description accessible before the box closes. The packer reports physical conditions; the facilitator compares wording. An assisted first use reveals an ambiguous readability condition, which returns to criterion construction and help.

**Use and change.** CHK.4 supplies answers from observations at 10:00, 10:05 and 10:10, entered at 10:12. At 10:15 the description changes to v3. Known unchanged v2 cards already mismatch it. If current cards may differ, current wording is instead unknown. The facilitator decides to keep v3 and replace the affected card, then obtains the changed comparison and any physical checks affected by handling. The old v2 answer remains historical.

**Worth and improvement.** A representative trial through [ME.11][ME11] observes whether the aid catches the wording problem, whether users can interpret the questions, and how much time or duplicated work it adds. [ME.14][ME14] compares that contribution with burden across the preparation work. A timely wording check can avoid reopening, replacing and repacking the set; completing the checklist faster is no gain if it misses that problem or merely moves the delay elsewhere. If a direct conversation at packing already prevents the omission with less cost, retain the conversation and retire the redundant aid. If the aid is useful but its description is hard to find, [ME.16][ME16] selects that focused improvement rather than enlarging the list.

Keep use, detected problems and work outcomes distinct. A caught wording mismatch is an observed contribution; it does not establish that the exercise would otherwise have failed. Another participant might have caught it later. Conversely, a session that went well does not establish that every check was sound. When appraising the change, account for the training, support, other changes and case differences accompanying the aid. Staff enthusiasm or a rising count of ticks does not isolate its effect.

The worked route uses CHK.1–4 with Method engineering; uncertain criteria or shared reliance bring in CHK.6 or CHK.5 when needed. It can return at several points: unsupported usefulness calls for domain inquiry; lost references call for template repair; inaccessible information calls for fitting; unchanged adequate grounds support economical reuse. The three physical-set answers never settle the exercise's usefulness by themselves.

## Shared work with uncertain criteria and changed premises

A rented-room workshop combines projection, card exercises and participant coordination. The technician uses a venue tool, the facilitator a materials workspace, and the organizer a session calendar. The team is uncertain whether “readable on screen” can be judged reliably at the technician's desk.

When local answers exist but their support for the session is unclear, [CHK.5](#chk5---reconcile-checklist-results-across-shared-work) first connects them to the shared result and exposes missing or conflicting contributions. Follow the return that answers the actual difficulty. In this case, uncertain projection checking calls for qualification before reliance on its verdict.

> **Mantra — from local answers to a shared result:** Name the shared result. For each contribution, recover the subject, question, conditions and grounds behind its answer. Reuse what is adequate; qualify uncertain checks and obtain what is missing. Ask what the whole still needs and whether the contributions can combine. Return a missing performer or resource to coordination, an unanswered subject question to the needed observation or interpretation, and incompatible claims to those who can resolve them. After change, retain unaffected grounds and reconsider dependent questions; after interruption, recover these distinct next moves. Use a conversation or an existing view when enough; record more only for a concrete later reliance.

The worked case below connects these moves to the room, materials and workshop. Stop reconciling when the shared question is sufficiently answered; the participants still make the continuation decision and perform the selected work.

**Qualification and selection.** CHK.6 challenges the criterion under the intended viewing conditions. A representative participant examines the actual projected example from relevant seats. If desk readability fails to distinguish a real difficulty, the team changes that criterion or its checking means. CHK.1 then retains questions about the room setup, actual content and exercise use; it leaves unrelated venue questions in the venue's own practice.

**Local representation and occasion.** CHK.2 preserves the session, room and materials references in the relevant local views. CHK.3 arranges the observation while the room and actual content are available. A missing capable interpreter returns to capability support; an unavailable room returns to scheduling.

**Local answers and simultaneous contribution.** Through CHK.4, the technician establishes equipment conditions and the facilitator compares projected and physical examples. The actual projection check contributes to equipment preparation and preparation of the workshop at the same time. Its relation to the whole changes what is checked: a test image alone cannot establish the actual example's use.

**Reconciliation.** CHK.5 connects the local answers to workshop W. A whole-session account includes the actual materials and arrangement, not a count of green local lists. If the facilitator and technician need the room at incompatible times, [OPS.4][OPS4] makes the conflicting claims visible to the people who can select a feasible arrangement before those contributions combine.

**Changed premise and continuation.** Moving W from room A to B reopens the room-dependent observations. Revising the example reopens its content and display questions. Known unaffected card facts remain usable. An absent technician assignment returns to coordination; an assigned technician with an unknown projection result returns to observation. After an interruption, the shared account lets participants recover these different next moves.

The route uses all six Checklist Methods because this constructed case has uncertain criteria, local forms, an occasion, actual answers and shared reliance. A simpler workshop may need only a conversation and a direct check. The example explains the connections; it does not prescribe six phases for every session.

# Sources and dependencies

## Source contributions and their limits

These sources inform the Methods in different ways. The historical and conceptual sources support problem recognition and synthesis. Empirical studies and engineering accounts support their stated observations under their own conditions.

| Source and return | Contribution used here | Limit and reconsideration condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| R7, Methodology, connected checklist passages in chapter 6 and their Method, qualification and change context | Questions about work subjects; reusable templates and filled instances; local adaptation; timing, assistance, skill, motivation and worth. | Translate the ideas under current FPF rather than importing meta-level or alpha terminology. Revisit the affected Method if a source distinction lost in translation changes use. |
| R10, Systems Management, connected operational model, shared-state and administration passages | Local interpretation, shared views, coordination and change in work involving several participants. | A shared representation does not establish performed work or the state of every subject. Revisit CHK.5 when the work arrangement changes. |
| Atul Gawande, *The Checklist Manifesto* (2009; 2010 UK edition), especially the professional-reminder, team-interaction and design/trial cases | Historical practitioner account of selecting attention and arranging real use. | Domain cases and suggested design heuristics do not establish universal list length, timing or causal effect. |
| [Urbach et al., 2014][URBACH] | A population-level implementation result constraining easy effectiveness claims. | Its before/after setting does not show that every checklist is ineffective. Seek domain-specific evidence when making an outcome claim. |
| [Facey et al., 2024][FACEY] | Mechanisms by which documentation can diverge from observed checklist practice. | One institutional setting does not establish prevalence elsewhere. Inspect the actual local arrangement. |
| [RLCF, version 2, December 2025][RLCF] | Criteria and checklist feedback in model training. | Training/benchmark results do not establish a deployed checker or current subject state. |
| [Selective Checklist Evaluation, EMNLP 2025][SELECTIVE] | Criterion-selection policy and evaluation setting can change judgement results. | No universal selection policy follows; agreement with judgements is not direct truth. |
| [AutoChecklist, version 1, March 2026][AUTOCHECKLIST] | Explicit generation, refinement and use of criteria for evaluation. | Reported experiments provide bounded support; local workflow and domain coverage still need examination. |
| [Anthropic, effective harnesses, November 2025][ANTHROPIC1]; [harness design, March 2026][ANTHROPIC2] | Observable completion checks, continuation across sessions and adaptation of evaluation means. | Engineering accounts depend on available models, tools and tasks. Reconsider the arrangement as those change. |
| [CheckPOINT, 2024](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37734956/); [Ridgeway et al., 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pecinn.2026.100495) | Observing interaction and distinguishing aid implementation from the practice supported. | Instrument performance does not establish outcome benefit. CHK.3 tests the intended interaction. |
| [Hölzing et al., 2026](https://doi.org/10.3390/clinpract16040069) | Simulation evidence distinguishes overall team behaviour from particular subscales. | The cohort overlaps an earlier technical-performance report; no independent clinical replication follows. |
| [Chen et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ergon.2023.103453) | Content and position cues for resuming interrupted work. | Student laboratory tasks limit transfer. Test the content needed for CHK.4's actual continuation. |
| [Hong et al., July 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.12835v1) | Coverage, granularity and uneven emphasis in generated rubrics. | A paper-reproduction benchmark and model-based evaluation support bounded comparison, not universal criteria. |
| [CHERRL, June 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.04923v1); [Rubric Dropout, August 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.11669v1) | Investigating exploitation of judge biases and divergence between optimized scores and intended results. | Experimental preprints; CHK.6 checks the receiving use. Training interventions do not prescribe ordinary omitted checks. |
| [SPECA, February 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.07513v1) | Transferring source-derived questions across implementations. | Its single audit and specification assumptions limit transfer. CHK.1 re-establishes applicability and grounds. |
| [Bagaria et al., August 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.02942v1); [RIPD, February 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.13576v1) | Sensitivity to question meaning and limits of benchmark validation after rubric edits. | Bounded preprints motivate CHK.6 contrasts, not universal failure rates. |
| [RuVerBench v2, September 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.29920v2); [PReMISE v1, May 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.30803v1) | Qualification of the actual judging arrangement in CHK.6. | Their benchmark and model-mediated results do not establish a universal grouping or voting rule. |

The useful synthesis is a short question set with recoverable meaning, an actual occasion and suitable grounds. A checklist does not supply all professional knowledge, prove that its described characteristics are useful, or establish a whole result merely through constituent passes.

This edition uses the supplying text identified in its first-edition source basis. A later date or a working hyperlink does not establish semantic compatibility. Before reusing an answer affected by a supplier change, compare the actual changed content with its named receiving use. Unaffected Methods remain usable.

## Refresh and improvement

Return first to the smallest affected contribution. A missed consequential question reopens CHK.1; lost meaning reopens CHK.2; unusable timing or access reopens CHK.3; unsupported subject answers reopen CHK.4; broken shared reliance reopens CHK.5; an inadequate criterion or checker reopens CHK.6.

Repeated non-use, prefilled answers, interpretation errors, burdens shifted to others and weak whole-result inferences can reveal defects in the aid or its arrangement. Use representative work and worth appraisal before expanding it. A changed source, model, tool or framework supplier reopens the dependent claim, not automatically the entire edition. Distinguish a changed way of working from a new release of its supporting tool: newer software does not by itself make the criterion or underlying Method better. Compare actual alternatives and their conditions of use. A new independently useful Method or a materially different human/AI practice boundary can justify reconsidering the framework's scope.

# Edition and citation

The public name is **Checklist Principles Framework**. **Checklist DPF** is a descriptive short form; **CHK** is its citation code.

Cite a pattern as “Checklist Principles Framework, CHK.4.” Add “first edition, 2026-09-25” when the reference selects this edition's body. CHK.1–CHK.6 identify the six practical answers collected here; their numeric order is a finding aid. A later title or publication-order change can preserve an identifier while the same practical answer continues. A split, replacement or retirement calls for an explicit reader return rather than reuse of the identifier for an unrelated answer.

This first edition covers the selection, construction, fitting, use, reconciliation and qualification of checklists in human, AI and mixed professional work. Its Readme, Preface, applications and source account support the same use. Its examples are constructed cases, and any claim of effectiveness in a particular field calls for evidence about that field and arrangement.

# Community Building Readme

## Practical entries

Use this framework when you are trying to make a useful cultural or community contribution: help people sustain a practice, obtain something from one another, take part in a valued activity, or make their shared experience useful elsewhere. A community organiser, participant, practitioner, sponsor or assisting agent can enter at the difficulty already present.

These are selected examples, not a catalogue or a coverage boundary. Bring the actual question to the [Table of Contents](#table-of-contents) when none fits. Open a pattern's Problem frame, then its Solution and worked case. You can ask an assisting agent: “Explain this and give me your comments in ordinary language, without framework jargon.”

### OFFER — Choose what would help

- **Situation:** You have been asked to start or grow a community, but people may need an existing resource, independent practice, expert help or company with one another.
- **Question:** Which contribution is worth making for these people under the available conditions?
- **First useful result or blocker:** A credible offer and a bounded action to obtain a response, or the particular missing contribution that prevents an honest offer.
- **Start with:** [CB.1](#cb1---choose-a-useful-cultural-or-community-contribution). Its comparison includes ways to develop carriers of a practice without requiring mutual communication.
- **Stop or return:** Keep an adequate existing arrangement. When the offer is sound and the remaining task is a first exchange, move to CB.2; when a professional method or permission is missing, obtain it from its actual supplier.

### EXCHANGE — Make one request lead to useful help

- **Situation:** People have joined a group, but a shareable question still has no relevant, willing contributor or useful answer.
- **Question:** How can this particular exchange be completed?
- **First useful result or blocker:** The recipient obtains a usable next step, connection or answer and returns what it helped them do, or the organiser identifies the unavailable expertise, material, access or time.
- **Start with:** [CB.2](#cb2---arrange-the-first-useful-exchanges). Use CB.5 when the difficulty is choosing and carrying out a richer contribution such as a case clinic or project review.
- **Stop or return:** An urgent accountable answer may require a service. Reconsider the offer through CB.1 when the central contribution repeatedly cannot be obtained.

### CONTINUE — Carry a voluntary activity through a change of organiser

- **Situation:** An organiser is leaving. People want some activity to continue, while access, funding or the right to decide remains unsettled.
- **Question:** What can continue, on whose terms, with whom actually able to perform it?
- **First useful result or blocker:** An agreed feasible continuation or ending. For a transfer, someone can take over and completes a first activity under the new arrangement; otherwise the missing mandate, capability or resource remains explicit. The useful activity, decision mandate, willing work with its means, first performance, settlement of what ends, and a return of what happened need to remain connected through the change.
- **Start with:** [CB.11](#cb11---continue-change-transfer-or-end-a-community-arrangement); use [CB.13](#cb13---establish-a-workable-mandate-for-shared-decisions) for missing mandate, [CB.7](#cb7---prepare-and-sustain-distributed-organising) for organising capability and [CB.9](#cb9---provide-for-community-work-and-agree-its-terms) for provision and terms.
- **Stop or return:** Reduce, pause or end an unsupported promise. Keep an adequate existing arrangement. An unresolved incident still needs its responsible receiver under CB.8.

## How to use the language

Use the method that answers your present difficulty. Choose the smallest contribution that can answer the situation, obtain its real inputs, perform the relevant work, and inspect what reached the intended person or action. The [Preface](#preface) explains how to connect methods and why the alternatives matter. The [Applications](#applications) show complete constructed uses across unlike settings.

The four Parts group related questions for finding them. They are not stages that every community must traverse. You can begin with a resource dispute, an incident, a missing contribution or a useful existing practice. Follow another pattern when you need its result. Permission refused, unavailable expertise or a burden that nobody accepts can stop the proposed action.

# Preface

## CB.Preface:1 - Useful cultural and community work

Community Building concerns the deliberate creation, support and renewal of useful participation, relationships and shared ways of working. Its wider cultural purpose can also be served by people who learn and use a practice independently. A population of carriers of a practice need not communicate, identify with a community or act as one decision-making body.

This language serves people constructing or changing such contributions in professional networks, voluntary groups, communities of practice, customer communities and other shared activities. The immediate difficulty may be an unclear offer, an unanswered request, inaccessible participation, exhausted organisers, a disputed rule, a missing shared resource, a practice that nobody can reuse, or a collective view that cannot reach a decision. People may also want more of an already useful activity. The framework helps turn that intent into something people can actually obtain and sustain.

Begin by distinguishing the intended change. A repairer may want a justified diagnostic continuation; a neighbour may want enjoyable company; a volunteer may need a manageable contribution; a sponsor may want more capable use of a product. Learning, relationships, cultural continuation and commercial outcomes can coexist, but one does not stand for the others. Their differences can change the offer, the appropriate method and who should bear its cost.

Use an existing satisfactory arrangement without re-engineering it. When one person needs a dependable professional answer, obtain the service. When an adequate explanation or learning provision lets people perform independently, that can be the whole cultural contribution. When there is no usable professional method, develop or obtain that method before promising its benefits. Community activity can help that work, but does not supply the missing domain knowledge by itself.

## CB.Preface:2 - What makes the choice difficult

People need a useful result without having unlimited time to help obtain it. Organising requires preparation, matching, access, follow-up and judgement, much of which remains invisible in an attendance count. A lively event can depend on unrepeatable founder work; a quiet resource can support valuable independent use. Count and visibility therefore answer only some of the practical questions.

Participation must fit different circumstances. Newcomers may need a small explained first action, while experienced members may need freedom to contribute occasionally. Recognition can acknowledge useful work, yet an unwanted public award can make participation harder. A sponsor may supply space or money while seeking control that defeats the participant's purpose. Volunteers can accept a bounded contribution without accepting a continuing production obligation.

Common work creates decisions about access, upkeep, rules and representation. The person who owns a room, the person who can teach a practice and the person authorised to speak for participants may be different people. Obtain permission from its holder, qualified help from a capable practitioner, and a mandate from those entitled to grant it. Keep an existing decision arrangement when it meets the shared need and provides appropriate consultation.

Evidence also has a cost. A returned account of one application may reveal a repair worth making. It does not estimate the prevalence of the problem or establish a general causal effect. Wider causal, learning or professional claims need the evidence appropriate to those claims. Choose that additional work when the decision depends on it.

## CB.Preface:3 - Connect the methods through the contribution needed next

Start from the working question and use any relevant results already obtained elsewhere. The following connections explain common choices; they do not prescribe a universal workflow.

[CB.1](#cb1---choose-a-useful-cultural-or-community-contribution) compares possible contributions and makes a credible offer. When mutual help is selected, [CB.2](#cb2---arrange-the-first-useful-exchanges) arranges a finishable exchange and obtains the recipient's account of its use. If the central contribution repeatedly cannot be obtained, reconsider the offer before recruiting more people. If the selected route is independent learning or a qualified service, obtain those contributions directly.

[CB.3](#cb3---make-entry-and-changes-of-participation-workable) makes a next participation action understandable and feasible, including a reduction, return or departure. [CB.4](#cb4---design-a-space-and-shared-activity-for-its-purpose) connects a space and shared activity to its intended result. [CB.5](#cb5---obtain-and-return-useful-contributions-from-participants) develops the actual contribution: a case clinic, a demonstration, a project review, joint work or another fitting form. A discussion setting supplies opportunities for interaction; prepared material, capable participants and the recipient's next use make that interaction useful.

[CB.6](#cb6---recognise-a-contribution-and-choose-a-meaningful-response) connects recognition to the contribution and the person's circumstances. [CB.7](#cb7---prepare-and-sustain-distributed-organising) obtains capable, supported organising work, including temporary participant groups where shared attention is needed, and an absence arrangement where continuity matters. [CB.8](#cb8---make-participation-rules-usable-and-resolve-incidents) makes expectations usable and carries incidents through judgement, response and correction. These methods address different problems: praise does not pay a promised fee, a role title does not prepare an organiser, and a welcoming tone does not settle a contested incident.

[CB.9](#cb9---provide-for-community-work-and-agree-its-terms) connects a promise to qualified time, access, funds and agreed terms. [CB.10](#cb10---understand-the-value-of-participation-and-cultural-work) examines particular uses and outcomes, including burdens, failures and unrealised potential, and returns a useful change. [CB.11](#cb11---continue-change-transfer-or-end-a-community-arrangement) uses those results to compare continuation, reduction, transfer, separation, pause and ending. An agreed transfer becomes effective when the receiver can perform the work and the former arrangement's obligations are settled.

[CB.12](#cb12---support-a-useful-repeated-action-of-participation) supports a wanted repeated action through a fitting occasion, feasible action and useful return. [CB.13](#cb13---establish-a-workable-mandate-for-shared-decisions) establishes a mandate where common decisions need one. Repetition is not the purpose of every participation arrangement; shared decision rights are not needed for every independent cultural use.

[CB.14](#cb14---develop-and-maintain-a-shared-repertoire-of-practice) develops a repertoire that practitioners can use, question and maintain. It can select simple documentation, reciprocal comparison or a properly provisioned development project. [CB.15](#cb15---connect-practices-through-a-useful-joint-contribution) connects practices through a useful joint contribution, keeping differences in meaning and working conditions visible. [CB.16](#cb16---form-and-carry-a-collective-voice-into-a-decision) carries a collective contribution into another party's decision with a position, mandate and returned answer. A useful idea can move between people without a joint method-development programme; an individual expert can speak without claiming to represent everyone.

When combining these contributions, establish their joint feasibility. An expert may be unable to advise on a case and welcome newcomers during the same hour; one room may not support two activities at the required time. Obtain another contribution, change timing or reduce the promise. An appeal concerning that expert's own response needs another reviewer; rescheduling alone cannot supply independence. Each local method may be sensible while the combination is impossible.

## CB.Preface:4 - Two ways to carry a practice, and why the distinction matters

An **arrangement based on mutual participation** makes contributions available through people working or spending time with one another. It may be a case exchange, music group, shared workshop or professional network. The arrangement must obtain suitable participants, material, interaction, support and a return to use. Its benefit can include valued relationships or an enjoyable experience; it need not be justified as a course or commercial acquisition mechanism.

An **arrangement for independent use** makes a practice obtainable and usable in people's separate settings. It may rely on a description, demonstration, exercise, tool and correction route. Cultural continuation then depends on actual acquisition, performance, selection and retention of the practice. A forum is optional. The [independent-use application](#application-3---extend-a-practice-without-a-discussion-group) shows how a missing resource changes this route even when the learner understands the method.

These alternatives can be combined within one person's changing participation. Someone can learn independently, ask one question, contribute an example and then return to private work. CB.3 supports that change when participation itself needs help. FPF Core's treatment of cultural evolution (C.36) supplies the wider distinctions among cultural transmission, performance, retention and renewal; CB.1 makes a particular cultural offer useful and feasible.

The language therefore starts from the receiving situation rather than a platform, a membership target or one inherited community model. It retains the useful organising repertoire found in practitioner sources while asking what each move contributes. Communities of practice supply powerful forms for joint learning and stewardship, yet learning together does not define every community or every cultural intervention. Business community methods supply purpose, provision and early organising constructions, while participants' own purposes and voluntary terms remain explicit.

This organization accepts some additional inquiry before choosing a format. It avoids committing people to recurring interaction when an adequate reference or individual service would suffice, and avoids publishing a resource as if it could replace the interpretation or relationship people actually need. When a new case defeats those alternatives, return to the particular contribution and its conditions, not to a universal claim that communities should grow or become more active.

## CB.Preface:5 - The work being performed, and the support it needs

A method in this book often describes a constituent of larger work. In the repairer application, asking for a discriminating observation is part of a peer exchange; that exchange is part of an attempt to obtain a diagnostic continuation; and the repairer's diagnostic work serves an actual customer's maintenance need. The customer commitment changes the peer exchange while it is happening. If the answer must be accountable and available within an hour, an optional evening group cannot carry that demand.

Another condition can change the constituent action without changing its conversational form. When the needed equipment record is confidential, the case owner first obtains permission or prepares a sufficient shareable case. A facilitator can support clarification but cannot replace the practitioner competent to interpret the observation. If that intermediate competence is absent, an orderly conversation still cannot produce the promised technical result.

The same relation applies to voluntary activity. Welcoming a newcomer may be part of running a garden session. Safe access to the shared tools, suitable supervision and the session host's available attention constrain the welcome. If the host must simultaneously resolve an urgent access incident, a prepared small task with another capable, willing helper may keep entry feasible; otherwise the session's promise must shrink.

Community Building provides only part of this work. The relevant practice supplies its professional method and correctness criteria. Human Capability Development (HCD) supplies development of a needed human capability and the conditions for practice and feedback. Organization Change Engineering (OCE) and Operations Management (OPS) help establish work arrangements and capacity when those contributions are missing; Management Accounting (MA) helps compare costs created by the chosen promise. Method Engineering (ME) and Research Method Practice (RMP) supply method development or research when those questions are open. The [supplier returns](#actual-supplier-returns) identify where those contributions become useful.

Replacing a contribution requires examining what it did in the whole. A written answer may replace an explanation of a known procedure while leaving a new case's diagnosis unresolved. Paying a coordinator may supply booking and material preparation while leaving expert capacity unchanged. Keep these differences visible when comparing alternatives and receiving the changed work.

## CB.Preface:6 - Recognise the problem, then establish the result

Recognition guides entry. An unanswered case suggests CB.2 or CB.5; recurring organiser overload suggests CB.7 or CB.9; a contested right to decide suggests CB.13. These observations do not establish that the selected arrangement works. Establish the result at the scope on which someone will rely.

For one combined use, ask:

- Who should obtain what, and do those people recognise the proposed benefit and participation terms?
- Which actual contributions, permissions and resources make that result possible, including preparation and follow-up?
- Can those contributions coexist at the required occasion, and who can change the promise when they cannot?
- What reached the next person or action? What remains an offer, a possible later benefit, a failed use or an unresolved question?
- Where do people obtain correction, change their involvement or decline an additional obligation?
- Which observed condition should reopen the offer, method, provision or continuation decision?

These questions inherit the detailed checks of the selected patterns. A new confidential case needs its own permission judgement; it does not require redesigning an otherwise adequate recognition practice. A changed room cost may reopen provision while leaving the diagnostic method intact.

The [worked applications](#applications) show the language's gain and cost. Organisers obtain more specific promises and can correct a failed condition; participants obtain clearer choices and usable contributions. The price is real preparation, follow-up and sometimes a smaller offer. The constructed cases explain decisions and operations. Evidence about the effects of using this pattern language would require field inquiry.

Whose account is easiest to hear can bias the result. Include a consequential missing perspective when a claim depends on it: a person who declined, a quiet user, a newcomer, an unpaid organiser or someone affected by a collective statement. Do not turn that inquiry into a demand for universal visibility. Ask for proportionate, permitted information and preserve useful disagreement.

## CB.Preface:7 - What this publication preserves and where to return

This publication selects sixteen recurring community and cultural work problems and develops methods for answering them. The complete bodies preserve their recognition conditions, construction, alternatives, worked cases, costs and return conditions. The ToC compresses each to a search row; the Readme compresses selected uses to entry guidance; the Preface explains connections. None of these compressed forms replaces the body needed to perform or adapt a method.

The source basis combines practitioner community-building accounts, the communities-of-practice repertoire, conceptual distinctions about culture and communities, bounded research contributions, and current FPF and domain-method suppliers. The [source-use account](#source-use-and-limits) states what was adopted, adapted or bounded and which changes would reopen it. Each body's SoTA-Echoing section gives the closer comparison and source return.

The framework deliberately leaves the full history and vocabulary of each source, platform-specific implementation, the complete professional methods used by a community, and the full learning, research or commercial product outside this edition. It also coarsens variation across local cultures and institutions. Return to the original source for a claim about its evidence or broader theory; to the domain supplier for work requiring its full method; and to the people and conditions of use before applying a general example as a local arrangement.

Unresolved use, repeated misunderstanding, changed provision or new source evidence should reopen the smallest affected method or relation. Inspect a proposed repair through the actual work and recipient result, including a contrasting condition that could defeat it. Wider causal or general effectiveness claims require further inquiry. The [renewal route](#renew-the-affected-contribution) keeps that work distinct from changing a link, publishing an edition or continuing the activity itself.

## CB.Preface:End

# Part A - Choose the contribution and make entry possible

## CB.1 - Choose a Useful Cultural or Community Contribution

> **Type:** Community-building method pattern
> **Status:** Stable

### CB.1:1 - Problem frame

Use this pattern when you want to help a practice spread, enable people to help one another, or create a place where a particular group can participate meaningfully, and the useful contribution is still unclear. A professional association proposes a forum; a neighbourhood organiser proposes a shared activity; a sponsor offers a platform. Before building the arrangement, determine whose situation it should improve and why this arrangement could do so.

Community Building covers both the development of people who carry a practice and the formation or continuation of relationships among participants. This pattern governs the choice of a contribution within that broad field. Its immediate subject is a proposed change in people's practice, participation or relationships and the arrangement that could support that change. People can adopt a practice without communicating with one another. Where mutual participation matters, its contribution needs an explanation of its own.

The first useful result is a bounded, understandable proposal: who could benefit, what would become possible, what participants and organisers would contribute, what conditions must hold, and which first action could test the proposal. A justified choice to use an existing service, improve access to a useful resource, or leave an adequate arrangement alone is also a result.

The intended user knows the activity in question or can obtain a qualified account from someone who does. This pattern helps organise a contribution; the activity's own professional methods supply correctness and specialist permissions.

**Ordinary non-use.** If an existing proposal already fits the people, purpose and conditions and the remaining difficulty is obtaining a first exchange, use CB.2. If one person needs help choosing a learning programme, use HCD.2. Return here when the proposed community activity itself may be the wrong response.

### CB.1:2 - Problem

An attractive community idea can hide several different problems. People may lack access to a reliable answer, opportunities to practise, trusted relationships, permission to use data, or a way to improve the practice itself. A discussion space addresses some of these conditions and leaves others intact. Its sponsor, active contributors and quiet participants may also want different results.

How can an organiser construct and compare useful contributions without treating a platform, shared label or sponsor objective as the answer?

### CB.1:3 - Forces

| Force | Decision it changes |
| --- | --- |
| A recognisable common concern | A sufficiently specific concern helps people decide whether to participate; a narrow description can also exclude people whose experience is needed. |
| Participants' benefit and organisers' purpose | A sponsor may sustain the arrangement, while its preferred behaviour may provide little value to participants. |
| Relationship and independent use | Some results need continuing mutual help; others can be obtained by people using an explanation or service independently. |
| Early uncertainty and credible commitment | A small practical probe can clarify the proposal, but participants still need truthful expectations about help, effort and control. |
| Diversity of situations and a feasible first action | One shared offer can contain several useful forms of participation; trying to serve every situation at once can prevent any exchange from working. |

### CB.1:4 - Solution

Start with one receiving situation, develop a small set of different ways to improve it, and make the chosen contribution concrete enough for affected people to question or try. Keep the cultural result, the mutual-participation result and the sponsor's result distinguishable.

**Working reminder:** find whose situation should change; compare ways to help; establish the needed contributions; make one honest offer; revise it from the response.

#### CB.1:4.1 - Recover the situation from people's work and experience

Ask a person who might use the arrangement to describe a recent relevant occasion. What were they trying to do or experience? What happened? Where did they turn, what did they receive, and what remained difficult? For an opportunity without a recent occurrence, retain the proposed situation as a hypothesis and say what makes it worth exploring.

Follow the detail that can change the proposal. A repairer saying “I need a community” may need help interpreting an unusual observation. Another may already know the diagnostic method but lack access to equipment data. A third may want colleagues with whom uncertainty can be discussed without embarrassment. These situations support different contributions even when all three people use the same occupational label.

Ask about existing help, including arrangements the organiser does not provide. A professional contact, a paid adviser, a manual, a local group or a private conversation can already answer the question. Establish what is missing from those alternatives before proposing another maintained activity.

Look beyond the founder's familiar contacts when their experience could misrepresent the intended use. Seek a consequential contrasting account: someone using another tool, working at another time, declining the original invitation, or facing a different access condition. Explain why their situation matters. This is purposeful inquiry, not a claim that a few conversations represent a whole population.

Use OCE.2 when the proposal depends on actual organisational work, informal help, access or authority that an organisation chart does not establish. Its result can show, for example, that the person everyone consults has no time allocated for that help. Preserve what the evidence establishes, what someone reports and what remains a proposal.

#### CB.1:4.2 - Separate the changes being sought

Describe each relevant change in ordinary language. Examples include being able to perform a known diagnostic procedure, obtaining a qualified second view on an unusual case, finding company for an activity, having one's experience heard, or developing a better practice with others.

For each proposed result, ask who values it and what would let that person recognise it. A participant can value a conversation or a sense of welcome without producing a document. In that case, ask about the experience under conditions in which an honest answer is possible. If the promise is improved professional work, obtain evidence about that work as well.

Keep three distinctions when they change action:

- **Access and capability:** possession of instructions or membership of a group does not establish that someone can use the practice.
- **Participation and relationships:** attending one event can be useful without creating a continuing relationship.
- **Participant and sponsor results:** product adoption or reduced support cost may matter to a sponsor, while the participant needs competent help or an opportunity to contribute.

These results can support one another. They need not be maximised together. Record a consequential disagreement rather than converting the sponsor's preferred measure into everybody's purpose.

#### CB.1:4.3 - Construct alternatives by how they would help

Generate alternatives that change the way the result is obtained. STR.5 supplies the fuller method for developing contrasting accounts of a worthwhile contribution and how it can be sustained. For a small community decision, compare the serious alternatives already exposed by the receiving situation.

| Receiving difficulty | A plausible arrangement | What must be available |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The answer is known and repeatedly needed | A usable explanation or maintained knowledge resource | Correct content, findability, an understandable scope and a way to notice outdated advice |
| A particular person needs a qualified answer under a dependable service commitment | A professional consultation or existing support service | Competence, a feasible response arrangement, access and an accountable provider |
| People need to perform a known practice independently | Suitable explanation, practice, feedback and access | A usable domain method, representative tasks, appropriate help and the conditions for later use |
| Different people hold useful experience and want to exchange it | A bounded mutual-help arrangement | Relevant requests, willing capable contributors, permissible material and enough coordination |
| People want continuing contact or shared activity | An accessible meeting or recurring shared practice | A purpose participants recognise, a workable form, welcome and an acceptable participation burden |

An existing adequate arrangement remains a serious alternative. Combine arrangements when each supplies a necessary contribution: a reference resource can answer routine questions while a small peer group handles unusual cases. Explain where the person changes route, so that “community support” does not become an unlimited promise.

Compare at the scale of the actual first use. Include preparation, response, correction, coordination and the participant's effort, not only platform cost. Do not make a well-developed favourite defeat an alternative described only by its name. Unknown willingness or capacity remains unknown until an appropriate response establishes it.

#### CB.1:4.4 - Build the contribution for the selected branch

For **mutual participation**, name the kinds of people whose contributions can help one another and the activity through which that help becomes possible. Describe the minimum relevant experience or access, the material people can bring, and what someone receiving a contribution will do with it. Membership criteria should follow the work and conditions of participation. A brand preference or friendship with the founder is insufficient when the promise concerns a wider professional group.

For **independent carriers of a practice**, identify the population and later activity to be changed. C.36 helps distinguish transmission, performance, selection and renewal of the practice. Then connect the needed contributions:

1. Make the useful activity and participation demand understandable to potential learners. Show a relevant use and the available means of learning it.
2. Establish that the domain method and its correctness criteria are available. If experts cannot supply a usable method, return that question to Method Engineering, and to Research Method Practice when unresolved evidence requires inquiry.
3. Use HCD.5 to select learning activities for the relevant starting conditions and HCD.6 to construct representative practice and changed-condition attempts. Obtain missing material, help or access through HCD.7/8; a teaching publication can use Learning Product LPF (local learning-publication practice; obtain separately).
4. Observe whether people can carry out the target activity under the support conditions of their later work. Keep course participation, helped performance and independent performance distinct.
5. Arrange how revised instructions, questions or observed failures can reach the people concerned. They may receive these from a provider without joining a discussion group.

This limited composition works when the professional practice is sufficiently known and the learning provision can actually be obtained. If the question is the design of a whole new service, return the contribution and delivery requirements to Systems Engineering. The organiser retains the question of whether the intended population can obtain and use the resulting provision.

#### CB.1:4.5 - Make an offer that people can assess

Express the proposal in language potential participants use. Include the situation it addresses, the benefit being proposed, the first activity, the contribution requested from them, and what the organiser or provider will supply. State the boundaries that could change their decision: time, cost, confidentiality, commercial interest, limits of help and a feasible way to decline or leave.

A conversation or short invitation can carry these contents. Make a distinction between a service that promises a response and a voluntary opportunity to ask capable peers.

Ask recipients to explain what they expect to do and receive. Then invite an appropriately small real action: offer a permitted case, choose an available learning attempt, attend a first shared activity, or explain why the proposal does not fit. Agreement with an appealing idea is weaker evidence than a response to its actual demands. A refusal can reveal an unsuitable condition; it does not by itself show that the underlying need is absent.

Where people depend on an employer or organiser, examine what declining would actually cost them. A nominally optional activity with adverse consequences for refusal needs a different participation account.

#### CB.1:4.6 - Choose the next action and a return condition

Continue when the contribution is sufficiently worthwhile and feasible for the bounded action being proposed. For mutual help, pass CB.2 the receiving situation, first useful result, willing participants or recruitment question, material and access limits, and available organising effort. For independent learning, pass the target work and provision conditions to the selected HCD use.

Stop or change the proposal when an existing alternative answers the situation better, a necessary contribution cannot be obtained, or the apparent common purpose hides a material unresolved conflict. An unanswered question can itself be the next useful result: who can provide the required access, whether the intended recipient values the proposed result, or whether any capable person wishes to help.

Reopen the smallest affected choice when later responses change the population, desired result, available competence, burden or terms of participation. One failed invitation does not require rethinking the whole cultural purpose; repeated inability to obtain the central contribution may.

### CB.1:5 - Archetypal Grounding

#### CB.1:5.1 - Independent repairers compare four ways to obtain help

This constructed case concerns twenty independent repairers who sometimes encounter unfamiliar equipment faults. A supplier offers a branded forum. Some repairers service competing products, and the supplier would prefer discussions that favour its own equipment.

The organiser first examines three stipulated accounts. One repairer spends time locating an already documented procedure. Another needs a second interpretation of an unusual observation. A third understands the procedure but lacks permitted access to the needed data. These accounts are enough to reject one undifferentiated promise of “faster repairs”; they do not estimate how frequent each difficulty is.

The organiser develops four alternatives. A maintained index to approved procedures could help the first person. A paid specialist could provide an accountable response to the second. A voluntary case exchange could also help that person when timing is flexible and suitable peers choose to participate. Neither discussion nor training supplies the third person's missing access.

The first proposal therefore combines a reference route with a small, brand-neutral case exchange. Its initial case must be shareable and within the participants' competence. The organiser explains the sponsor's involvement, permits relevant discussion of other brands and obtains agreement on what material can be retained. If the sponsor requires promotional control inconsistent with that promise, the organiser changes the sponsorship arrangement or narrows the offer honestly.

The offer is: bring one permitted diagnostic question; a small group will try to identify a justified next step during an agreed window; the case owner will report whether that step was usable. It promises a bounded attempt at peer help. It does not promise repair completion or a guaranteed response to every future case.

CB.2 receives that proposal. An urgent customer case requiring a dependable specialist response uses the service alternative instead.

#### CB.1:5.2 - More carriers without a discussion group

The same association wants more repairers to recognise one well-understood fault condition. In this constructed variant, the diagnostic method, correctness criteria and authorised training examples already exist.

The organiser makes the use and prerequisites understandable, obtains a demonstration and a practice task through the relevant HCD methods, and ensures that repairers have access to the required information in their own workshops. A changed example tests whether they can select and use the diagnostic procedure under the stated help conditions. The training provider collects fault reports and distributes corrections to the material.

This arrangement can produce the intended cultural contribution even if the repairers never talk to one another. If their remaining difficulty is interpreting genuinely new cases, the organiser can later compare peer exchange and expert consultation. If the method itself is unsettled, more enrolments would not settle it; that question returns to method development.

#### CB.1:5.3 - A voluntary activity changes the criterion of usefulness

Neighbours want a quiet place to read and talk together. The proposed result is enjoyable company and an accessible opportunity to participate. The organiser asks about timing, travel, noise and the kinds of conversation people welcome. A smaller nearby meeting may fit better than a large online group.
